lich.ghi_chu_gio_ty: The Zi hour of a day runs from 23:00 the night before to 00:59; the 23:00–23:59 slot tonight already belongs to tomorrow's Zi hour (see tomorrow's page).

lich.nam.cach_tinh: The Vietnamese lunar calendar is computed astronomically for Hanoi time (UTC+7): the first day of a month is the day of the new moon, and the leap month is the first month in the year without a major solar term. The Chinese calendar uses UTC+8, so some years differ by a day or a month.
lich.cn.kl.loi: In lunar year {n} the {vai} is {tuoi} by the traditional age count, which falls on {kl} — folk custom usually avoids weddings then; many families borrow someone else's age or move to the following year.
lich.cn.ln.loi: In lunar year {n} the {vai} is {tuoi} by the traditional age count and falls on {xau} — folk custom often has someone of another age stand as owner for the ground-breaking or the move-in.

Clashing months and unfavourable age years are checked only for the main people (bride, groom, owner); days with these notes still appear, ranked lower.
lich.cn.gt.nguon: Xieji Bianfang Shu (1741), volume 36 — the section on wedding months by the bride's sign; the book records the rule and then calls it groundless
lich.cn.gt.loi: Folk calendars sort wedding months by the bride's sign. For a bride born in a {con_giap} year, the greatly favourable months are {dai}; the lesser favourable months are {tieu}. Months here follow the solar terms (the Tiger month is the first month), so a calendar printed by lunar months may differ by a few days around the start of a month. The very almanac that records this sorting says it has no basis, so the system only adds a label for families to consult — it never uses it to rank or drop a day.
